/u/Brother_tempus summed up my thoughts nicely on the 2nd Amendment, so I shall simply address the "Should we actually expand the definition of 'arms' (is a computer virus a type of 'arm' in this age of technology)? " angle.

I don't think computer virii should qualify as "Arms" under the second amendment. Here's why...Historically, "Arms" has typically meant weaponry which is meant to directly and immediately cause harm upon a person's body when used against them by another person. Therefore, a "Use of Arms" inherently carries with it the implication, or at least the threat, of imminent harm to self. Theoretically speaking, if I brandish a pistol, I am assaulting you due to the threat of the use of deadly force. If I come at you with a billy-club, it is well-understood that if you do not do something to either respond in kind or run like hell, that you are going to end up in a world of physical pain and medical peril. The use of violent force and the intent to do harm to a very specific person are important determining factors in these crimes. If I infect your PC with a virus...what direct physical harm have I done you? I have caused economic harm, yes, as you now must either spend time or money getting your PC repaired/cleaned (Unauthorized Access/CFAA). The virus may have stolen your banking details, which were sold to a third party who then drained your bank account (Theft/Larceny) But there is no direct threat to your person or personal safety, as a result of said virus. Even in a case where a person has hacked a smart-car and say, causes a crash...the virus itself is not a weapon, it is simply the means by which the crash was caused, as it is the precise instructions the virus contains, rather than simply the act of being a virus, that causes the scenario that begins the crash. It is no more a weapon than, say a pair of snips for cutting a brake-line or a wrench for loosening lug nuts would be. The person is still allegedly guilty of assault with intent to cause great bodily harm, but the precise means here matters very little, compared to the intent.

In this vein, I see little difference in calling a virus a "Weapon" or "Arms", than Sarkeesian claiming all of this criticism of her online amounts to "Defamation" simply because it gives her a horrible reputation. Sure, both cause theoretical harm to a person, but the means by which they cause harm (Sarkeesian is a lying and intellectually dishonest pundit seeking to push an agenda, and people don't like punditry dressed up as scholarism/Virii cause economic harm, not direct physical harm upon a person's self) is important for proper legal classification of the crimes allegedly involved in the cases.
